subject: Action Required: 14 Employees Missing Section 2 I-9 Verification
snippet: Marcus, Our monthly scan of Vireo Health Systems' I-9 records found 14 employees hired between May 26 and June 4 who do not yet have a completed Section 2 (Employer Review and Veri
body_text:
Marcus,

Our monthly scan of Vireo Health Systems' I-9 records found 14 employees hired between May 26 and June 4 who do not yet have a completed Section 2 (Employer Review and Verification) on file. Federal law requires Section 2 be completed within three business days of the employee's first day of work for pay. All 14 of these employees are now past that window -- the earliest, Marcus Alvarez in Facilities, is 23 days overdue as of this email.

This is flagged as a compliance risk, not just a paperwork gap. Penalties for substantive I-9 violations currently run $281 to $2,789 per form for a first offense, and ICE has been more active with I-9 audits in the healthcare sector this year specifically -- we've seen three of our other client systems get audit notices since January. Given Vireo has 200 employees and a multi-site footprint, a full audit would not be a quick fix.

Full roster with hire dates and due dates is attached (i9_section2_roster.csv). Please note seven of the fourteen are in Nursing -- if this is a pattern of new hires starting on the floor before HR paperwork is finalized, that's worth addressing at the workflow level, not just clearing this specific backlog.

What we need from you:
1. Assign a reviewer (you, Renata, or Claudia) to complete Section 2 for all 14 employees. The employee must present original identity and work-authorization documents in person -- this cannot be done remotely for any of these.
2. Log completion in the I-9 Advantage portal as each one closes out so our next scan reflects it.
3. If any of these employees no longer have their original documents available, flag them back to us immediately -- there's a different remediation path (Form I-9 Section 3 rules don't apply here, but late-completion documentation does).

We are recommending you treat this as resolved-in-full by July 15. If you want a call to walk through the highest-risk cases first (the three that are already 3+ weeks overdue), reply and we'll get 20 minutes on the calendar this week.

For context, this is the second consecutive monthly scan where the Nursing department has accounted for the majority of new findings -- four of the six flagged in May also cleared late, past their original three-day window, just not late enough to trigger last month's report. If June's fourteen resolve on time but the pattern repeats in July, we'd recommend a short process review with whoever handles new-hire paperwork on the floor, since the gap looks structural rather than a run of one-off misses.

Portal: https://portal.i9advantage.com/vireohealth/dashboard

Best,
I-9 Advantage Compliance Team
compliance@i9advantage.com | (855) 555-0199

body_text:
You have been invited to the following event.

Title: Onsite Interview: Dana Whitfield -- VP, Clinical Operations
When: Mon Jun 29, 2026, 1:00 - 4:00pm, Mountain Time
Location: Vireo HQ - Boardroom / Video for remote panelists
Guests: Marcus Bell, Doug Feinstein, Dr. Elaine Ford, Priscilla Nam

Description:
Onsite panel for Dana Whitfield, our first finalist for VP, Clinical Operations. Background below for prep -- please read before Monday.

Dana is currently Senior Director of Clinical Operations at Meridian Health Partners in Colorado Springs, where she's run a 140-bed multi-site ambulatory network for the last four years. Fourteen years in healthcare ops total, starting as a floor RN before moving into administration. MBA from University of Denver, 2016. She led Meridian through a joint-commission survey with zero conditional findings last cycle, which is the single biggest thing on her resume that maps to what we need here -- Doug flagged our own survey readiness as the #1 gap in the VP Clin Ops role when we scoped it back in May.

Panel and rotation (all times Mountain):
1:00 - 1:45 Doug Feinstein (VP Clinical Operations, hiring manager) -- role scope, reporting structure, how she'd approach the first 90 days
1:45 - 2:30 Priscilla Nam (Director of Nursing) -- staffing model, nurse retention (this is the one area she's lightest on -- Meridian's turnover was actually higher than ours last year, so push on this)
2:30 - 2:45 break
2:45 - 3:30 Dr. Elaine Ford (CEO) -- strategic alignment, board-facing comfort level
3:30 - 4:00 Marcus Bell -- comp expectations, close

Comp: we're positioned at $185-205K base plus 15% bonus target. Her current base per the recruiter is $178K so there's room, but she mentioned equity/PTO buyback matters to her more than base -- worth surfacing in your slot if it comes up naturally.

Scorecards are due in Greenhouse by end of day Monday so we can debrief Tuesday morning before she flies back. Dana Whitfield is also a finalist at two other systems per the recruiter, so we are not the only game in town here -- if the room likes her, we should move fast.

Resume and Greenhouse profile: https://app.greenhouse.io/candidates/1180432
Questions before Monday, just call or Slack me.

One more thing worth flagging before the room: her references (two direct reports, one peer director) all independently used some version of the word 'decisive' unprompted, which tracks with the 90-day plan she sent ahead -- it's more concrete than most candidates give us at this stage, down to which committees she'd sit in on in week one. If the group has concerns, better to surface them Monday than after an offer's on the table.

subject: Re: Night/weekend shift differential — proposal
snippet: Ran both scenarios against current headcount and the open reqs Priscilla flagged. Full model attached, but here's the summary. FTE-only scope (benefits-eligible night/weekend nursi
body_text:
Ran both scenarios against current headcount and the open reqs Priscilla flagged. Full model attached, but here's the summary.

FTE-only scope (benefits-eligible night/weekend nursing staff): annualized cost of the proposal is about $284,000 above current differential spend, based on 96 FTEs currently working qualifying shifts. That's a real number but it's inside the nursing labor variance we're already tracking against budget this year, mostly because we've been running those three reqs open and backfilling with agency staff at a much higher effective rate — agency nurses on nights are running us close to $95/hr loaded versus roughly $58/hr loaded for a differential-adjusted staff RN. So there's a real argument this pays for itself if it closes even two of the three open reqs within two quarters.

FTE+PRN scope: adds another $61,000 annualized for the roughly 22 PRN nurses who pick up qualifying shifts regularly. Smaller number than I expected, honestly, because PRN utilization on nights specifically is lower than I assumed going in.

My recommendation, purely from a numbers standpoint: include PRN. The incremental cost is modest relative to the FTE base cost, and excluding PRN creates an obvious incentive problem — PRN staff would have every reason to decline night/weekend shifts once FTEs are getting paid more for the same work, which undermines exactly the flexibility PRN is supposed to give us.

One flag for budget planning purposes: this isn't currently in the FY26 labor budget as modeled in January, so if approved it needs a formal budget line adjustment, not just a payroll config change. I can draft that adjustment once you have a final scope and effective date. Happy to walk through the model live if useful.

Lena Cho
Senior Financial Analyst, Vireo Health Systems

snippet: Tim, Marcus — Here's my full scorecard from both onsite loops, since I know Priya — sorry, Priscilla — wants the detail before she weighs in. Dr. Renee Castillo — Strategy & Vision
body_text:
Tim, Marcus —

Here's my full scorecard from both onsite loops, since I know Priya — sorry, Priscilla — wants the detail before she weighs in.

Dr. Renee Castillo — Strategy & Vision: 4.7/5. She walked through how she took her current system from two regional clinics to eleven in under three years, including the change-management pain points, which is exactly the phase we're entering with the West expansion. On the operations side she was noticeably thinner — when I pressed her on how she'd handle a night-shift staffing shortfall at a single site, she gave a fairly generic answer about escalation paths rather than specifics. Culture fit: good energy, direct communicator, a little polished for my taste but that's a minor note. References were strong — her CNO called her 'the reason our expansion didn't fall apart.'

Anthony Vogel — Strategy & Vision: 3.6/5. Solid but not visionary; he thinks in terms of the next two quarters, not the next three years, which is fair given his current scope. Operations: 4.9/5 — the best operational interview I've sat in this year. He walked the panel through an actual staffing crisis at Aurora last winter, the exact levers he pulled, and the follow-up process changes. He knows our EHR quirks, our union contract nuances, and half the nursing leads by name already. Culture fit: excellent, obviously, he's been here four years.

My honest read: if we're hiring for the next 18 months of just running the region well, it's Anthony, no contest. If we're hiring for the next five years of scaling into new markets, Castillo has a higher ceiling but real ramp risk. I don't think this is a slam dunk either way and I'd rather we argue it out before we make an offer than regret it in six months.

One more data point that didn't fit neatly into a score: I asked both of them the same closing question — 'what would you do in your first 30 days?' Castillo talked almost entirely about stakeholder mapping, a listening tour across the new sites, and a 90-day strategic plan she'd present to Elaine and the board. All reasonable, but it's the answer of someone who's done this at a company with a much bigger management layer underneath her, where thirty days of listening doesn't leave anything on fire. Anthony's answer was narrower and more tactical — shadow the highest-turnover unit for a week, fix the two scheduling bottlenecks he already knows about from his current seat, then start the conversation about the new sites. Neither answer is wrong, but they tell you which job each of them thinks they're walking into, and I'm not convinced either of them has fully absorbed that this role is genuinely both.

Curious to hear Priscilla's read from the nursing leadership panel before we go further.

Doug Feinstein
VP, Clinical Operations
Vireo Health Systems

subject: Fill your open RN roles in 14 days — CareStaff Partners
snippet: Hi Marcus, My name is Deborah Klinger and I run healthcare partnerships for CareStaff Partners in the Mountain West region. I wanted to reach out directly because we've been workin
body_text:
Hi Marcus,

My name is Deborah Klinger and I run healthcare partnerships for CareStaff Partners in the Mountain West region. I wanted to reach out directly because we've been working with several health systems in the Denver metro this year who are dealing with the same story: RN vacancies staying open 60-90+ days, agency spend climbing to cover the gap, and a permanent hiring pipeline that just can't keep pace with turnover.

I don't know the specifics of what Vireo Health Systems is dealing with, but given your size (roughly 200 employees, if our data is right) and the general environment for clinical hiring in Colorado right now, I'd guess you're feeling some version of this. A few things that have worked well for organizations like yours that we partner with:

1. A dedicated 'gap coverage' contract that guarantees a minimum number of credentialed RNs on 30-day notice, so you're not scrambling every time someone gives notice.
2. A conversion pathway — travelers and per-diem staff who want to convert to permanent roles do so at a fixed, pre-negotiated placement fee (typically 15% of first-year salary), which tends to be far cheaper than a search firm and results in people who already know your floors and your team.
3. Credentialing handled entirely on our side — license verification, background checks, competency testing — so your People Ops team isn't doing double work when a traveler starts.

We currently support four health systems in the Front Range with a combined 60+ active placements, and our average time-to-start for an RN med-surg or ICU role is 9 days from signed contract to first shift.

One more data point that might be useful regardless of whether we ever work together: across our Front Range partners, the single biggest predictor of whether a traveler converts to a permanent hire isn't pay — it's whether they get a real orientation to the unit's specific workflows in the first week, versus being treated as plug-and-play coverage. Units that assign a dedicated preceptor for the first five shifts see conversion rates roughly twice as high as units that don't, even when pay and schedule are identical. It's a small operational fix but it seems to matter more than almost anything else we track.

I'd love 20 minutes to hear what your current staffing model looks like and whether there's a fit. No pressure either way — happy to just share our Denver-market rate card if that's more useful right now.

Best,
Deborah Klinger
Regional Partnerships, CareStaff Partners
(303) 555-0177 | solutions@carestaffpartners.com

body_text:
Team --

Kicking off the Q3 performance cycle today, and I want to walk through what's different this time before Lattice starts sending you automated reminders that won't explain the why.

The biggest change: we're moving from a single year-end review to two lighter check-ins (Q3 and Q1) plus the annual comp conversation staying at year-end. Last year's engagement survey was pretty blunt that a once-a-year review cycle meant people were getting feedback on things that happened nine months earlier and had already forgotten the context. This isn't meant to double your workload -- the Q3 check-in is intentionally short. Three questions, no forced rating, no calibration meeting attached to it. Its whole job is to surface anything that needs to change before year-end, not to be a formal record.

Key dates:
- Self-reflections open in Lattice: July 20
- Manager check-ins due: August 14
- Skip-levels for anyone flagged 'at risk': by August 21
- No calibration session for Q3 -- that stays a year-end-only exercise

What I need from each of you specifically:
Doug and Priscilla -- your clinical teams are the largest population and the ones most likely to find yet another HR system annoying. I'd rather you tell your managers this is genuinely short than have them find out the hard way and disengage from the next one too. If your directs push back on timing given the Unit 4B situation, tell them to talk to me directly rather than you absorbing that.

Omar -- Lattice SSO has been flaky for a subset of clinical staff logging in from shared workstations. If that's not fixed before July 20 we're going to have a rough launch. Can you confirm status by end of week?

Jenna -- no payroll action needed this cycle, comp conversations stay at year-end as usual. Flagging only so Q3 doesn't show up as a surprise line item anywhere.

Claudia, Tim, Renata, Farida -- you'll each get manager-facing FAQ content from me by the 18th to pre-empt the obvious questions. If something comes up in the meantime that you can't answer, send it my way rather than guessing -- I'd rather field ten questions from you than have inconsistent answers circulating on the floor.

Happy to walk any of you through this individually if it's easier than absorbing it over email. My door's open.

One more thing, since I know someone will ask: this cycle is separate from the annual comp conversation, and separate from the calibration process year-end uses. If your team members ask whether a Q3 check-in affects their raise this year, the honest answer is no, directly -- but the trend it surfaces could absolutely inform what we talk about at year-end, so it's worth taking seriously rather than treating as a formality to click through.

Marcus Bell
Head of People, Vireo Health Systems
(720) 555-0142

body_text:
Marcus,

Pulled together themes from the last six exit interviews on the inpatient units, and I think there's a pattern worth acting on rather than just filing away.

Three of six cited scheduling rigidity specifically — not the schedule itself, but how little flexibility there is to trade shifts or adjust for family stuff without going through a formal request that sometimes takes a week to get approved. Two mentioned float pool assignments feeling arbitrary, like they're pulled with no notice and no say in which unit. And four of six brought up pay, specifically that travel nurses on their same units are making considerably more for the same work, which is a hard thing to sit with day to day.

None of this is shocking, but six exits in a quarter on units that used to be pretty sticky is more than normal churn. I'd like to partner with HR on something more concrete than the engagement survey action items we did last year, which honestly didn't move much. Do you have bandwidth to think this through with me before it gets worse?

Priscilla

body_text:
I'm inclined to approve this, but let me actually walk through my reasoning rather than just say yes, since the sign-on pool is one of the line items the board asked us to hold the line on this year.

Danielle is exactly the profile we struggle to hire for — a nurse manager with real turnaround experience, not just tenure. Priscilla doesn't oversell candidates lightly, and the fact that she's pushing this hard tells me something. Losing her to a competing offer over a $3,000 gap on a role we've had open for four months would be a bad trade against basically any reasonable measure of cost. The PTO exception doesn't concern me at all — that's squarely a manager-discretion call and exactly the kind of thing I want Marcus and Priscilla deciding without escalating to me.

The sign-on number is where I want to be careful, not because $2,500 is a large sum in isolation, but because of precedent — if this gets discussed among other nurse managers, and it will, I want us to be able to defend it as a genuine market-driven exception rather than something that looks arbitrary. So here's what I'd like: if Finance confirms the sign-on bonus pool has room this quarter without pulling from a line we need elsewhere, approve up to $7,500 — splitting the difference rather than giving her the full $8,000 ask, framed to her as 'we moved as far as we could on sign-on and gave you everything you asked for on PTO and start date.' If Finance says the pool is tight, come back to me and we'll figure out a non-cash sweetener instead — extra CME budget, a later performance review date for her first raise eligibility, something along those lines.

One more thing while I have you both: I'd like recruiting to start tracking counter-negotiation patterns across the nurse manager and director-level reqs specifically, separate from our normal offer-acceptance metrics. My sense, and it's only a sense right now, is that we're seeing more candidates counter on sign-on and PTO than we did eighteen months ago, which either means our base offers have quietly fallen behind market or it means candidates have gotten more sophisticated about negotiating, or both. If it's the former I'd rather fix the base-offer numbers proactively than keep granting one-off exceptions that are individually defensible but collectively look like we don't know what the role is worth. Tim, can you pull the last six months of nurse-manager-and-above offers and flag which ones needed an exception like this one, and roughly how big? Doesn't need to be formal, just want a gut check before comp planning season.

Let's not lose her over $2,500 either way, but let's do it in a way we can defend later.

Elaine Ford, MD
CEO, Vireo Health Systems

snippet: Happy to help get this on rails. Here's the process I'd recommend, at a high level. First, keep the leave determination and the accommodation determination conceptually separate ev
body_text:
Happy to help get this on rails. Here's the process I'd recommend, at a high level.

First, keep the leave determination and the accommodation determination conceptually separate even though they involve the same employee. The leave piece is largely mechanical once you have a certification — confirm FMLA eligibility (12 months of service, 1,250 hours, which given a 200-person employer you're almost certainly covered for), get the medical certification form back within the standard window, and track the leave against the 12-week allotment the normal way. Nothing unusual there procedurally.

The accommodation piece is where I want you to slow down. Once the employee is cleared to return with restrictions, that triggers the ADA interactive process independent of the FMLA leave tracking. That means: get the specific functional restrictions in writing from the treating provider (not a diagnosis — just what tasks are and aren't restricted, for how long), have a real conversation with the employee about what accommodations they believe would work, and separately have the department head assess what's operationally feasible in that role. Document each of those three inputs separately, because if this ever gets scrutinized the thing regulators and plaintiffs' counsel look for first is whether the employer actually engaged in a good-faith, documented back-and-forth rather than just approving or denying unilaterally.

On workers' comp: only relevant if any portion of the underlying condition is claimed to be work-related. If the employee hasn't filed a claim, don't volunteer that theory — but if it comes up, loop in Gail at Fairhaven immediately since that triggers separate reporting obligations.

A couple of process notes that will save you headaches later. First, whatever accommodation you land on, put an end date or a re-evaluation date on it even if the restriction letter doesn't specify one — open-ended accommodations are the single most common thing I see turn into a dispute eighteen months later, because nobody remembers to revisit them and then it looks like either an informal permanent change to the role or, worse, like you forgot the employee existed. Second, if the department head's operational-feasibility assessment concludes something isn't workable, get that in writing too, with the specific operational reason, not just 'doesn't work for the team' — vague denials are what get second-guessed later, specific ones generally hold up fine. Third, resist the urge to solve this entirely over email once the paperwork starts moving; a short call with the employee to walk through the plan tends to land better than a written offer appearing out of nowhere, even when the substance is identical.

Practically: Claudia, get the certification and restriction paperwork moving. Once you have the functional restrictions in hand, send them to me before you propose anything to the employee — I want to sanity-check the proposed accommodation against the restrictions before it's offered, not after. Should be a quick turnaround on my end, typically 24-48 hours.

Happy to get on a call if a conversation would be faster than email for any of this.

Josh Lieberman
Bramwell LLP | Employment Counsel
(303) 555-0166

snippet: Marcus, Wanted to give you the full picture on where we landed with the internal I-9 audit before we're both in the compliance committee meeting Monday, since there's a fair amount
body_text:
Marcus,

Wanted to give you the full picture on where we landed with the internal I-9 audit before we're both in the compliance committee meeting Monday, since there's a fair amount to absorb and I'd rather you have it in writing than get it cold in the room.

We pulled a full sample — every I-9 on file for anyone hired in the last three years, 187 forms total — and ran it against the current USCIS requirements as part of the proactive self-audit outside counsel recommended after the sector-wide enforcement uptick this spring. The good news is the vast majority are clean. The part that needs real attention: 14 forms have Section 2 completed more than three business days after the employee's start date, which is a technical violation regardless of whether the documents themselves were valid. Six forms are missing a List B or List C document reference entirely — just blank fields where something should have been recorded. And two forms, both from the same hiring wave in early 2025, have document expiration dates that were never followed up on, meaning we may currently have expired work authorization on file without a reverification on record.

None of this looks like anything intentional — it reads like inconsistent onboarding process across the two people who were handling Section 2 before Renata took it over full-time last year, which honestly tracks with what I'd expect given how that responsibility bounced around. But 'unintentional' doesn't change our exposure if ICE or DOL ever came knocking, and self-identified, self-corrected issues are treated very differently than issues found by an examiner, which is the whole point of doing this now rather than waiting.

Outside counsel's recommendation, and mine, is that we build a full remediation package: corrected I-9s where we can still legally correct them, a documented timeline of when the errors were identified and how they're being fixed, updated the two expired-document cases immediately with proper reverification, and a revised internal process so Section 2 always has a single owner going forward. I've drafted most of the narrative already, but I need your sign-off on the process changes and Renata's help pulling the two reverification cases together, since those are time-sensitive.

Where I need something from you specifically: comfort level with the proposed narrative on the process gap, and a confirmed point of contact for the two live reverification cases. Committee wants a full response package ready by August 15th, which sounds tight but is genuinely doable if we can lock in the process language this week.

Let me know if you want to grab time before Monday to walk through the actual sample data — happy to bring the spreadsheet.

Farida

Marcus,

Full picture on the internal I-9 audit before Monday's compliance committee meeting.

Sample: 187 forms, last 3 years. 14 late Section 2 completions, 6 missing List B/C references, 2 unresolved expired-document cases.

Recommendation: full remediation package, response due August 15.

Farida

snippet: Marcus, Time to start planning for the 2027 plan year, and there's more moving this cycle than last year so I want to walk through it in detail rather than just dropping a rate she
body_text:
Marcus,

Time to start planning for the 2027 plan year, and there's more moving this cycle than last year so I want to walk through it in detail rather than just dropping a rate sheet on you.

Medical: Vireo's PPO renewal came in at a 6.2% premium increase, which is in line with what we're seeing across our book of business in healthcare services this year given continued cost trend in the Denver market. Employee-only PPO premium moves from $210/month to $223/month; family coverage moves from $612 to $650. I know that's a real number for a lot of your lower-wage staff, so we should talk about whether Vireo wants to absorb any of that increase rather than passing it through in full — happy to run scenarios at 25%, 50%, and 100% employer absorption if that's useful for budget planning. I can have those scenarios modeled against this year's actual enrollment mix within a few days of you giving me the go-ahead, so we're not guessing at the cost impact when we present options internally.

New this year: we're adding an HDHP option paired with an HSA, which should help on the premium side for employees who don't need first-dollar coverage. Employee-only premium on the HDHP is $84/month, and I'd recommend Vireo seed the HSA with an employer contribution — $500 for employee-only, $1,000 for family coverage is a common design and would meaningfully drive adoption in year one.

Dental and vision are renewing flat with Delta Dental and VSP respectively — no action needed there beyond standard re-enrollment.

FSA limits are moving to $3,300 (up from $3,200) per IRS guidance, and HSA limits move to $4,400 individual / $8,800 family. I'll have the updated plan documents reflecting all of this by mid-September.

On timing: I'd recommend an enrollment window of November 1-15 for coverage effective January 1, 2027, which gives us a comfortable runway before year-end. I'd like to propose a kickoff planning meeting for the week of August 3 so we can nail down the communication plan, benefits fair logistics, and get the census file moving early enough that there are no surprises when open enrollment opens.

Can you confirm a date that works, and let me know who on your team should own the census file pull this year? Last year that came from Renata and it went smoothly, so happy to keep that arrangement if she's available again. I'd also like to get on your calendar for a short readout with your leadership team once we've locked the plan design, since questions about the HDHP option tend to land better coming from someone who can speak to the total comp picture rather than just the benefits mechanics.

Best,
Angela

subject: Manager Calibration Guide: Q3 Cycle -- Action Needed by Aug 1
snippet: Hi Marcus, With manager reviews closing July 24 and calibration starting July 27, here's the full walkthrough for how ratings should move through calibration this cycle -- please f
body_text:
Hi Marcus,

With manager reviews closing July 24 and calibration starting July 27, here's the full walkthrough for how ratings should move through calibration this cycle -- please forward the relevant sections to your calibration leads if you haven't already.

Rating distribution guardrails: we are not using forced ranking, but Lattice will flag any team where more than 35% of ratings land in the top bucket (Exceeds) or more than 15% land in the bottom bucket (Needs Improvement) for a manual second look. Last cycle, Clinical Operations came in at 41% Exceeds, which is what triggered the calibration conversation with Doug in Q2 -- worth getting ahead of that again this time rather than surfacing it after ratings are already communicated to employees.

Calibration session structure (recommended, not mandatory):
1. Each manager brings their draft ratings and a one-line justification per direct report, focused on the outliers (top and bottom) rather than walking every single person.
2. The calibration lead (typically the department VP) facilitates -- goal is consistency across managers reporting into the same function, not consistency across the whole company.
3. Any rating change made in calibration should be logged with a reason in the notes field so the manager has something concrete to say in the actual review conversation.
4. Compensation conversations should NOT happen inside calibration -- keep merit/promotion discussion in a separate follow-up, otherwise the rating conversation quietly turns into a budget conversation and ratings get anchored to what the department can afford rather than actual performance.

Known friction points from last cycle that we've heard about already:
- Nursing managers want more calibration time given they each have 12-15 direct reports vs. the company average of 6. We've pre-booked a 90-minute nursing-only calibration block on July 28 instead of folding them into the general clinical session.
- A few managers were confused last cycle about whether self-review responses are visible during calibration. They are not, by design -- calibration should be manager-driven, self-reviews come back into play during the 1:1 conversation.

Timeline recap:
Jul 15 -- self-reviews due
Jul 24 -- manager reviews due
Jul 27-28 -- calibration sessions (nursing gets its own block on the 28th)
Aug 1 -- ratings finalized in Lattice, released to managers for delivery conversations
Aug 1-8 -- 1:1 review conversations should be completed

Full guide with screenshots: https://lattice.com/admin/cycles/q3-2026/calibration-guide

Let us know if you want a live walkthrough with your calibration leads before the 27th.

-- The Lattice Team

subject: HR Brew: Why nurse burnout is reshaping retention strategy
snippet: Good morning, THE BIG STORY: Why nurse burnout is reshaping retention strategy A new joint survey from the American Nurses Foundation and a coalition of health system HR leaders fi
body_text:
Good morning,

THE BIG STORY: Why nurse burnout is reshaping retention strategy

A new joint survey from the American Nurses Foundation and a coalition of health system HR leaders finds that 41% of bedside nurses say they're 'somewhat' or 'very' likely to leave their current role in the next 12 months — up from 34% two years ago. The reasons aren't primarily about pay. Staffing ratios, mandatory overtime, and a perceived lack of voice in scheduling decisions top the list.

What's working: health systems that have stood up formal 'staffing escalation' processes — a defined, fast path for a charge nurse to flag an unsafe ratio and get a response within the shift, not the following week — report meaningfully lower turnover among tenured nurses (3+ years). Several HR leaders we talked to this month said the escalation process mattered more to retention than sign-on bonus size, which tracks with what we've seen reported elsewhere.

ALSO IN HR THIS WEEK

- Pay transparency: two more states have introduced legislation requiring salary ranges on all job postings, bringing the total to 14 states plus DC. If you hire remote or multi-state, it's worth checking whether your postings already comply with the strictest state you touch.

- AI in hiring: the EEOC issued informal guidance clarifying that employers remain liable for adverse impact caused by AI screening tools, even third-party ones. Several readers wrote in asking whether this changes anything practically — short answer, it reinforces existing obligations rather than creating new ones, but it's a good prompt to audit whatever screening tool you're using.

- Benefits: open enrollment season is around the corner for calendar-year plans. Early data from brokers suggests average premium increases in the 7-9% range for 2027, driven mostly by specialty drug costs and GLP-1 utilization.

- Comp: a growing number of mid-size employers are moving to twice-yearly comp reviews instead of one annual cycle, citing retention pressure in competitive labor markets. Early data is mixed on whether it actually moves the needle versus just adding administrative overhead.

WORTH YOUR TIME
A deep dive on how three regional health systems restructured float pools to cut agency nurse spend by 20-30% without increasing core headcount. Read it here: https://hr-brew.com/stories/float-pool-restructuring

READER MAILBAG
A People leader at a 250-bed hospital system wrote in last week asking how other HR teams are handling exit interviews for clinical staff, given how time-strapped charge nurses and unit managers already are. The most common answer: a short, five-question async survey sent automatically on the employee's last day, with a live exit interview reserved only for RNs with three or more years of tenure or anyone flagged as a regret loss by their manager. A few readers noted this cut their exit-interview completion rate roughly in half in terms of raw volume, but nearly doubled the completion rate among the tenured group specifically — which is the population most HR teams actually care about for retention analysis anyway.

That's it for this week — see you Thursday.

— The HR Brew Crew

subject: Benchmark report: How healthcare orgs compare on engagement
snippet: Hi Marcus, We just closed out our 2026 mid-year benchmark analysis, pulling engagement survey data from more than 210 healthcare and healthcare-services organizations on Culture Am
body_text:
Hi Marcus,

We just closed out our 2026 mid-year benchmark analysis, pulling engagement survey data from more than 210 healthcare and healthcare-services organizations on Culture Amp, ranging from 50 to 5,000 employees. I wanted to share the highlights directly since Vireo Health Systems ran its own engagement survey with us back in Q1, and several of these trends line up closely with patterns we're seeing across your peer set.

First, the headline number: average engagement across healthcare organizations sits at 68% this year, down two points from 2025. The drop is almost entirely concentrated in frontline clinical roles — nursing, in particular, is down five points year over year, while corporate and administrative functions actually ticked up slightly. Manager relationship and workload/burnout questions are the two categories dragging the overall score down the hardest. Organizations that scored well on both tend to share a few practices: skip-level check-ins at least once a quarter, a formal process for escalating staffing-ratio concerns, and manager training that specifically addresses recognition, not just performance management.

Second, retention. Voluntary turnover among RNs across our healthcare cohort averaged 19.4% this year, essentially flat versus last year, but the organizations in the bottom quartile for engagement had turnover north of 27%. The correlation between engagement score and RN retention is stronger this year than any year we've measured it, which suggests engagement work isn't just a nice-to-have right now — for organizations fighting a nursing retention problem, it may be one of the more cost-effective levers available, especially compared to sign-on bonuses, which our data continues to show have a weak effect on 12-month retention.

Third, a smaller but interesting finding: organizations that shared survey results back with employees within two weeks of close (versus the more typical 4-6 weeks) saw participation rates in the following cycle rise by an average of 11 points. Speed of communication seems to matter more than the specifics of what's communicated.

I'd like to walk you through the full report and, if useful, pull a custom cut comparing Vireo's Q1 results against this healthcare-specific benchmark rather than our all-industry default. Given the nurse retention conversations I know are live for you right now, I think the RN-specific slice would be the most actionable part.

One more thing worth flagging: we also broke the data out by tenure band this year for the first time. Engagement among staff in their first 90 days is actually quite high across the cohort — averaging 76% — but it falls off sharply between month 6 and month 18, which is a pattern we don't see nearly as strongly outside healthcare. A few organizations we work with have started running a dedicated 'stay interview' at the six-month mark specifically to catch that dip before it turns into a resignation, and early results look promising, though the sample size is still small enough that I'd call it a trend to watch rather than a proven fix.

Happy to send the raw benchmark deck ahead of any call if that's easier than scheduling something cold — just let me know which is more useful.

Let me know if a 30-minute review call works sometime in the next couple of weeks.

Best,
The Culture Amp Research Team

Marcus,

Writing to formally notify you of a complaint that came in through the confidential ER hotline on August 1, filed against the Unit 4B charge nurse supervisor. I want to walk you through where this stands and how I'm planning to run the investigation, and get your sign-off before I go further given the sensitivity.

The complaint alleges unfair scheduling retaliation and a pattern of hostile communication directed at the complainant during team meetings, following a disagreement over shift coverage several weeks ago. I want to be careful here not to characterize this as more or less serious than it is before we've actually done the investigation — the allegation is specific enough to warrant a full process, and I'm treating it that way.

I've already completed the required steps: acknowledged receipt to the complainant within our 2-business-day standard, and sent a preservation notice to IT and to the Unit 4B manager to hold all scheduling records, relevant email correspondence, and meeting notes covering the last 90 days. Nothing gets touched or reorganized until this closes out.

My planned timeline is attached in detail, but at a high level: I'll interview the complainant this week, interview the subject with counsel present the following week, and interview three witnesses the complainant identified, all before reviewing the scheduling logs for the disputed period side by side with what I hear in the interviews. I'm targeting a findings memo and recommendation to you and Elaine by August 21.

A few things I need from you:
First, sign-off that this timeline and process is appropriate given what we know so far — I don't want to be three interviews in and find out you wanted a different approach.
Second, I'd like Josh Lieberman looped in before I interview the subject, since there's a real possibility this ends in disciplinary action and I want the process to hold up if it's ever challenged.
Third, I need your help keeping this contained — the complainant specifically asked that this not become unit gossip, and Unit 4B is a small enough team that containment is going to be hard without deliberate effort from both of us.

I'll send weekly status updates regardless of whether there's material news, just so this stays visible. I'd rather over-communicate on this one than have you hear about developments secondhand from Doug or from the unit itself.

Last thing — I want to flag that I'm treating the complainant's identity as confidential even internally beyond what's strictly necessary for the interview list. If you need to know who filed it for any reason, come to me directly rather than asking around; I'd rather that information stay as contained as the rest of the record.

Claudia

snippet: Hi Marcus, Results from the Q3 Engagement Survey (closed August 1) are ready. 182 of 200 employees responded -- a 91% response rate, the highest we've seen this year and up from 84
body_text:
Hi Marcus,

Results from the Q3 Engagement Survey (closed August 1) are ready. 182 of 200 employees responded -- a 91% response rate, the highest we've seen this year and up from 84% in the spring pulse.

Headline numbers:
- Overall engagement: 76% favorable (+2 pts vs spring)
- eNPS: +22 (+4 pts)
- Manager effectiveness: 73% favorable (+2 pts)

Department breakdown is the more interesting story this time. Nursing came in at 68% favorable -- still the lowest of any department, though up 17 points from spring's 51%. Given everything that's gone into the retention push this quarter (the new shift-swap policy, the RN case manager backfills, the calibration conversation Doug and Priscilla have been having), that movement is meaningful, but nursing is still 8 points behind the next lowest department (Clinical Ops at 74%) and 16 points behind Corporate/Admin at 84%.

Verbatim comment themes worth reading closely: scheduling flexibility came up 41 times as the top negative theme (down from 58 mentions in spring -- the shift-swap pilot appears to be landing), followed by career pathing (33 mentions) and pay transparency (19 mentions). On the positive side, team camaraderie (58 mentions), clinical autonomy (37), and leadership accessibility (29) all scored well, and leadership accessibility specifically was up sharply from spring -- likely reflects Dr. Ford's town halls landing well.

Full report with all verbatims and department cuts is attached (q3_engagement_summary.pdf). I'd suggest sharing the department-level numbers with Doug and Priscilla directly before this goes any wider -- the nursing trend line is good news but the gap is still real, and how it gets framed in a broader all-hands matters.

A couple of secondary cuts worth a look before that conversation: engagement by tenure shows the usual U-shape, with employees under 6 months and over 5 years both scoring above average, and the 1-3 year band scoring lowest company-wide at 69% -- that band is also where we're seeing the most voluntary attrition per the numbers Wendy in Finance pulled last month, so the two data sets are at least directionally consistent. Manager-level engagement (i.e. how engaged people managers themselves report being, as opposed to their teams) came in at 70% favorable, four points below individual contributors -- worth keeping an eye on given how much weight the calibration guide puts on manager judgment this cycle.

One flag on methodology: this was the first cycle using the shortened 24-question survey instead of the old 40-question version, so trend comparisons against anything before Q1 2026 should be read with caution -- the shorter instrument tends to run a couple points more favorable across the board per Culture Amp's own benchmarking notes.

Interactive dashboard: https://app.cultureamp.com/reports/q3-2026-engagement

-- Culture Amp

subject: Updated handbook — Colorado & Nevada multistate provisions
snippet: Team, Wanted to get this in front of all of you before it goes out more broadly, since you're the ones who'll be fielding questions from your teams once it's live. Josh finished hi
body_text:
Team,

Wanted to get this in front of all of you before it goes out more broadly, since you're the ones who'll be fielding questions from your teams once it's live. Josh finished his review of the Colorado and Nevada language yesterday, so we're clear to roll out the updated handbook sections this week.

The short version: both states have specific paid-sick-leave accrual rules that differ from our existing PTO policy language, and Nevada in particular has a separate 'any reason' leave requirement that isn't tied to illness at all. Rather than try to write one policy that awkwardly covers every state, we've added state-specific addenda that sit alongside the core handbook — so the base policy doesn't change for anyone outside Colorado or Nevada, and employees in those states get an additional section that spells out exactly what applies to them.

A few things worth knowing before people start asking:

For Colorado: the accrual rate is one hour of paid sick leave per 30 hours worked, capped at 48 hours per year, and it can roll over up to 48 hours into the following year. This is slightly more generous than what our general PTO policy provides in isolation, so for Colorado employees the addendum effectively sits on top of existing PTO rather than replacing any of it.

For Nevada: employees accrue 0.01923 hours of leave per hour worked, which nets out to about 40 hours a year for a full-time employee, and it can be used for literally any reason without needing to disclose why — no doctor's note, no explanation required. HR will handle tracking this separately from PTO in the system so it doesn't get commingled.

None of this changes anything for employees outside those two states — this is purely additive compliance work, not a broader policy shift, so please don't let it turn into a rumor that PTO policy is changing company-wide, because it isn't.

Rollout plan: the updated sections go live in the employee handbook portal Friday morning. I'll send a short all-staff note the same day pointing people to the changes, but I wanted you all to have the substance first so you're not caught flat-footed if someone on your team reads it before the announcement goes out. If you're managing anyone in Colorado or Nevada specifically, take a few minutes to read the addendum yourself — happy to walk through it live if that's easier than reading it cold.

Questions, come find me before Friday.

Marcus

body_text:
Team,

I've had a chance to sit with everything Rich sent over, and I want to walk through my thinking before Marcus and Rich move on the offer, because I know this isn't the direction most of us were leaning two weeks ago.

When we first got the slate, I was genuinely torn — Dr. Castellano's clinical background is a better direct match for what Priscilla's team needs day to day, and Doug's read on her interview was strong. I said as much on the 29th, and I meant it. If the reference checks had come back clean, I think we'd be sending her an offer today.

But they didn't come back clean, and I don't think we can talk ourselves past what two independent references told Rich separately: three departures from her direct reports in eighteen months, both references describing it as connected to how she managed performance conversations rather than normal attrition. That's not a single data point I'm willing to write off as noise, especially walking into a department that's already short-staffed and where Priscilla and her charge nurses are stretched thin as it is. If we bring in a leader who compounds that turnover problem, we're not solving the thing we hired this role to fix — we're making it worse, and we'll be back here in twelve months hiring again, except with a nursing staff that's more burned out and more skeptical of leadership changes than they are today.

Tran's references, by contrast, were about as strong as I've seen — both former direct reports specifically brought up retention and coaching without being asked, which tells me something. He doesn't have quite the same depth of acute clinical operations experience as Castellano, but he's run larger teams, and Doug, you flagged in your first note that the operational chops were there even if the clinical specialization was a step down from hers. I'd rather ramp someone up on the clinical specifics with support from Priscilla's team than inherit a retention problem in a department I can't currently absorb more turnover in.

So: let's go with Tran. Marcus, can you have Rich prep the offer — I'd like to get it in front of him by early next week if we can, given he mentioned a competing process. And Marcus, can you and Doug talk about how we let Dr. Castellano down — I want that handled cleanly and with real respect for her time; nothing about her candidacy was disqualifying in the abstract, this came down entirely to what came back in the reference calls, and I don't want that message to get muddled into something it isn't.

Thanks all for the thorough work on this one — I know it's not the outcome most of us expected a couple weeks ago, but I'd rather make the harder call now than the easier one and regret it in a year.

Elaine

Anthony is the safer choice and probably the more popular one on the floor, and if this were a backfill of Doug's role I'd sign off on the committee's vote without a second thought. But it isn't. The board approved this headcount specifically for the West region build-out, and Tomás — sorry, wrong board, I mean our own board — approved it on the premise that we'd bring in someone who has actually built a multi-site region from scratch, not someone who is excellent at running the one we already have. I know this contradicts where we landed as a group last week and I don't take that lightly. But I'd rather eat the awkwardness of overriding now than the cost of getting the West build-out wrong. Extending the offer to Dr. Castillo — Tim, can you get that moving today? And someone needs to have the Anthony conversation before he hears about the offer secondhand.

Elaine Ford, MD
